documents: Stich, Casado Rabasco, Madiedo, Guerrero Rascado & Morales Soto (2022), Seismic observation and location of a meteor burst from a dense station deployment in southern Spain, Geophysical Research Letters 49, e2022GL099999 (published PDF, 9 pages; Supporting Information not supplied)

entry.evidence: Eyewitness accounts mention an audible boom, ground vibration or tremor, and windows rattling at several places in the province of Granada.

sequences.source_document: Stich et al. 2022, GRL, published PDF

steps.action: Report the 11 December 2016 bright meteor seen by meteor cameras and news and eyewitness accounts of a boom and felt ground vibration in Granada.
steps.quote: Eyewitness accounts mention an audible boom, ground vibration or tremor, and windows rattling at several places in the province of Granada.

steps.action: Set the aims: tell ballistic from explosive signals, locate the terminal explosion in the actual atmosphere, compare with optical data, and assess wavefield variability over short distances.
steps.quote: The recordings are used to distinguish between ballistic and explosive signals, locate the terminal explosion considering the actual atmospheric conditions

steps.action: Inspect waveforms from 68 IAG and IGN stations and find a conspicuous signal between 21:28 and 21:32 UTC.
steps.quote: Following up the eyewitness reports of ground vibration, we examine regional seismograms for signs of airwave coupling to ground motion.

steps.action: Use the conditions found during the live event: a dense temporary 30-station broadband transect (Tropical Profile, ~3.5 km spacing, uniform installation) lay within the detection zone.
steps.quote: The temporary deployment consists of a dense, E-W trending transect of 30 seismic [...] .

steps.action: Establish that the signal is an atmospheric acoustic arrival: ~0.4 km/s apparent velocity across the network, visible on vertical and horizontal components at 44 stations.
steps.quote: Such velocities near the acoustic wave speed corroborate the origin from an atmospheric perturbance.

steps.action: Identify N-shaped displacement (W-shaped velocity) pulses and pick arrival times at the onset of the principal wave package.
steps.quote: We use velocity and displacement waveforms to assign arrival times at the onset of the principal wave package in the recordings.

steps.action: State two rival sources: a disintegration event acting as an isotropic point source, or the ballistic conical shock wave of the entry.
steps.quote: could be related to one of the disintegration events visible on video recordings of the meteor fall, or to the ballistic shock wave

steps.action: Take from published theory the rivals' predictions: circular arrival isochrones for a point source, elliptical or hyperbolic ones for a conical shock front.
steps.quote: In this case, the arrival time isochrones on the ground are expected to show a circular pattern

steps.action: Compare the interpolated isochrones (Delaunay triangulation of picks, incomplete to the northwest) with the predictions; they show circular arcs, provisionally favouring a disintegration event.
steps.quote: describe circular arcs (Figure 1), with no notable elongation, suggesting an origin from a disintegration event.

steps.action: Locate the source by atmospheric ray tracing and particle swarm search in BAM, with ERA5 temperature and wind at 21:00 UTC as the propagation model.
steps.quote: The location and time of the seismically recorded fragmentation event is estimated from the atmospheric ray-tracing and source search algorithms

steps.action: Vary the inversion settings: swarm populations, random seeds, and fixed versus free origin time; results are equivalent.
steps.quote: convergence of the search appears robust for different random seeds

steps.action: Obtain the source at 37.47°N, 3.92°W, 38.4 km altitude, 21:25:47.2 UTC, with a 5.0 s mean absolute residual and residuals below 10 s within ~5 km of the best solution.
steps.quote: yielding the source of the wavefield at 37.47°N, 3.92°W, altitude 38.4 km and origin time 21:25:47.2 UTC

steps.action: Check non-detecting stations JAND (83 km N) and ESTP (87 km W) against the predicted shadow zone; their silence is consistent with a shadow-zone limit shifted southeast by the wind.
steps.quote: without detection of the meteor signal, suggesting that the limit of the shadow zone is shifted toward the southeast

steps.action: Compare the inverted origin time with the time of maximum luminosity on camera records (21:25:47.3 UTC); they agree within a ±10 s resolution.
steps.quote: The inverted origin time compares favorably to the time of maximum luminosity, although the resolution of this parameter is low

steps.action: Since azimuthal coverage and short-distance data cannot discriminate spherical from conical geometry, design a new test: compare source height with the optical trajectory (burst height versus height zero for a cone).
steps.quote: we cannot verify if isochrone fragments (Figure 1) correspond to spherical or conical wavefield geometry

steps.action: Triangulate the luminous trajectory from five SMART meteor cameras with AMALTHEA (98.7 km to 18.5 km, bearing N309°E, 57° incidence) and identify 13 brightening events.
steps.quote: Triangulation of the meteor trajectory places the start of the luminous phase at 37.290°N, 3.617°W and altitude 98.7 km

steps.action: Compare the seismic source with the optical trajectory: the 38.4 km height maps to 37.519°N, 3.960°W on the trail, close to the seismic epicentre, as the point-source rival predicts.
steps.quote: comparing favorably with the seismic location (Figure 3)

steps.action: Keep the result that the signal comes from an explosive fragmentation event at 38 km height radiating a quasi-spherical shock wave.
steps.quote: So far, the analysis could clarify the origin of the incoming acoustic signal from an explosive fragmentation event at 38 km height

steps.action: From the simplest single-N-wave records (TP04, TP11, TP27), exclude source multiplicity as the cause of complex waveforms; only one (the most luminous) fragmentation event radiated significantly.
steps.quote: more complex waveforms and multiple N-wave arrivals at other stations cannot be attributed to the source, but must represent propagation effects

steps.action: Pose the question of how much local propagation and coupling effects contribute to variability over ~3.5 km station spacing.
steps.quote: offers an unique opportunity to evaluate the variability of the recordings over short distances

steps.action: Measure signal strength, durations, spectral peaks and three-component polarization along the transect (Figure 4).
steps.quote: we measure signal strength, duration and spectral characteristics on vertical component waveforms, and instantaneous signal polarization

steps.action: Compare horizontal polarization with station azimuth; the 43° mean residual is near random, unlike earlier meteor cases showing an outward-propagating front.
steps.quote: corresponding to a mean absolute residual of 43°, close to the expected value for a uniform distribution of angles

steps.action: Propose topographic echoes (TP22 second bundle) and diffracted waves near the shadow-zone edge as explanations of polarization and incidence variability.
steps.quote: can be attributed to an echo, possibly reflected from topography SW of the station

steps.action: Describe the along-transect pattern: order-of-magnitude scatter in amplitudes and frequencies, a long-wavelength trend only in duration, and a stable ~2 Hz displacement peak frequency.
steps.quote: of which only the signal duration shows a long wavelength component to the variations

steps.action: Attribute gradual duration changes to atmospheric multipathing (path effect), and frequency and amplitude scatter to site effects including buildings (TP07) and topography, drawing on published mechanisms.
steps.quote: The gradual variation points to a path effect

steps.action: Conclude that the origin time matches maximum luminosity and that camera triangulation confirms the seismic location with reasonable agreement.
steps.quote: confirm the seismic location of the principal fragmentation event by triangulation from regional meteor cameras with reasonable agreement

steps.action: Assign the remaining seismic-optical discrepancy to auxiliaries (atmospheric model uncertainty, diffraction into the shadow zone), not to the point-source claim.
steps.quote: [...] could be introduced by uncertainties in the atmospheric model, or the effects of diffractions

steps.action: Exclude a seismically recorded ballistic shock wave.
steps.quote: No seismic coupling has been found for the ballistic shock wave from the meteoroid passage.

steps.action: Keep the explanation that waveform complexity arises from receiver-side topographic scattering and multipathing through small-scale atmospheric structure.
steps.quote: We attribute this characteristic to local topographic scattering at the receiver site as well as to multipathing through the small-scale structure of the atmosphere

tree.answer: Yes: an acoustic-seismic signal of the meteor at 44 local stations, established by its ~0.4 km/s apparent velocity
No: the source position and time are latent and inferred by ray tracing through ERA5
Locate the terminal burst, tell explosive from ballistic source, characterize short-distance variability
Point-source disintegration event versus ballistic conical shock; later, source multiplicity versus propagation and site effects
Yes: circular versus elliptical isochrones; source height at the burst versus height zero
Found: one live event recorded by a temporary transect that happened to be there

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: No: a single event; the repetition is across stations, not across events
Location robust to swarm settings and origin-time treatment; agrees with independent camera triangulation; non-detections fit the shadow zone
Point source at 38.4 km kept as the principal fragmentation event; ballistic coupling not found; complexity attributed to path and site effects
No review file supplied; acknowledgments say two reviewers' suggestions were incorporated

end.claim: The seismic arrivals at 44 near-field stations are consistent with a point source at 38.4 km height (37.47°N, 3.92°W, 21:25:47.2 UTC; 5.0 s mean residual, ~5 km and ±10 s resolution), matching the most luminous fragmentation event on the camera trajectory.

decisive_move.sentence: Ray-tracing source location through the ERA5 wind and temperature model in BAM produced the 38.4 km point-source estimate that was then compared with the camera trajectory and origin time.

gates.evidence: The data came from permanent networks and a temporary transect deployed for other purposes, so no hypothesis directed the acquisition. The seismic source height could have fallen off the optical trajectory (a conical shock aligns with height zero), and the authors announce this check in advance (p. 3: ' [...] this assumption again later by comparing the seismic location to camera recordings'). Nothing was fixed before the data were seen: the search volume was set from the observed isochrones (p. 4).

imports.item: particle swarm optimization for source search (Bonyadi & Michalewicz 2017)
Delaunay triangulation (Shewchuk 1996) to interpolate arrival-time isochrones
ray theory, effective sound speed, diffraction and creeping waves beyond the shadow zone (Pierce 2019)
ideal-gas adiabatic sound speed with heat capacity ratio 1.4
SMART meteor camera network and AMALTHEA planes-intersection trajectory triangulation

novelty_claims.quote: Acousto-seismic coupling of the near-field pressure wave has been recorded by an unusually large number of 44 local seismic stations.
meteor events that have been recorded in the near-field at several tens of local stations remain a rare exception
offers an unique opportunity to evaluate the variability of the recordings over short distances

limits: Supporting Information (Figures S1-S3, waveforms, polarization, inclination) was not supplied, so steps citing it rest on the main-text description. No review file was supplied; the acknowledgments say two reviewers' suggestions were incorporated, but which changes they forced cannot be coded, so there is no review sequence. The arrival-picking procedure and its uncertainties are not quantified; no uncertainty is given for the camera triangulation, so 'reasonable agreement' is not scored against a tolerance. Only one atmospheric model (ERA5) is used; no alternative atmosphere is tested, so its stated role in the residual discrepancy is untested (inference). Sub-claims: the explosive rather than ballistic origin is a best_explanation (the isochrone test was inconclusive and the decisive evidence is the height comparison with a single independent data set). That only the most luminous fragmentation event radiated is a best_explanation ('presumably', p. 6). Attribution of waveform complexity to topographic scattering and atmospheric multipathing is a best_explanation, offered as plausible without modelling. The along-transect patterns (duration trend, ~2 Hz displacement peak) are descriptive regularities from one event. Composition none_fits: a single live event, estimation-led, with one rival test against independent optical data. It is not a trace series of independent events, not nature's repetition, and the dense transect is not a new capability. Triangulation (computed) is not met: the only full checks of independent kind are replications against the camera data; the robustness checks vary inversion settings only.

disagreements.support: Polarization along the dense transect deviates from station azimuth by a 43° mean absolute residual, near random, so the outward-propagating front reported for earlier meteors is not reproduced here.
disagreements.quote: [...] meteor examples (Langston, 2004; Pujol et al., 2005; D'Auria et al., 2006), the acousto-seismic polarizations of the 2016 Granada meteor do not [...]

alternatives_considered.reason: Circular isochrone arcs and source height falling on the optical trajectory near the brightest event

alternatives_considered.chosen: Origin time free in the inversion
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Origin time fixed at 21:25:47.3 UTC (maximum luminosity)
alternatives_considered.reason: Free origin time gives equivalent results

alternatives_considered.reason: To prevent the temporary deployment from dominating the result

alternatives_considered.reason: To cover diffracted arrivals beyond the geometric shadow zone
